questions.question: A 62-year-old weighing 84 kg is selected for fibrinolysis for STEMI. Using the standard adult STEMI weight-tier regimen without an older-patient dose reduction, what is the tenecteplase dose?
options: 40 mg as a single IV bolus
45 mg as a single IV bolus
50 mg as a single IV bolus
25 mg as a single IV bolus
questions.explanation:
Weight-Based Tenecteplase for STEMI

Correct answer: 45 mg as a single IV bolus

Use the Indication-Specific Weight Table

**The standard STEMI tenecteplase regimen uses weight tiers rather than one fixed dose for all adults.** At 84 kg, the applicable tier is ==45 mg==.

Check the vial, reconstituted concentration and delivery instructions. A dose stated in milligrams should not be converted to milliliters without confirming the preparation.

Do not substitute an acute ischemic stroke regimen merely because the drug name is the same.

Complete the Fibrinolysis Prescription

**The lytic is only one component of treatment.** Appropriate antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy, monitoring and immediate transfer are also required.

The ESC 2023 fibrinolysis recommendation advises considering half-dose tenecteplase in patients older than seventy-five years. Thus an otherwise eligible older patient in the 80-to-below-90-kg tier would receive 22.5 mg under that modified regimen, rather than the standard 45 mg. The sixty-two-year-old in this stem is outside that age modification. Keep the guideline age wording and local protocol explicit rather than confusing this reduction with a stroke dose.

Review contraindications, weight reliability, recent antithrombotic exposure and bleeding risk before administration. Observe for neurologic symptoms and other bleeding after treatment. A correct numerical dose does not establish that the patient was eligible for fibrinolysis or that reperfusion succeeded. Assess the subsequent ECG and clinical response and use the rescue or planned angiographic pathway as appropriate. Keep indication and protocol visible in the prescription to prevent confusion between different tenecteplase uses.

Body weight | Standard STEMI dose

<60 kg | 30 mg

60 to <70 kg | 35 mg

70 to <80 kg | 40 mg

80 to <90 kg | 45 mg

≥90 kg | 50 mg

40 mg as a single IV bolus: Forty milligrams is the standard STEMI tier for weight at least 70 but below 80 kg; this patient weighs 84 kg.

50 mg as a single IV bolus: Fifty milligrams is the standard maximum tier for weight at least 90 kg, rather than the 80-to-below-90-kg tier supplied here.

25 mg as a single IV bolus: Twenty-five milligrams is not the standard full-dose STEMI tier for this patient; it can arise in a different indication or an explicitly modified regimen.

ESC ACS guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad191

questions.question: A 68-year-old is receiving STEMI fibrinolysis and aspirin. There is no P2Y12 contraindication. Which oral P2Y12 regimen matches the 2025 ACC/AHA recommendation at fibrinolytic administration?
options: Ticagrelor 180 mg loading, then 90 mg twice daily
Clopidogrel 75 mg daily without a loading dose
Clopidogrel 300 mg loading, then 75 mg daily
Prasugrel 60 mg loading, then 10 mg daily
questions.explanation:
Clopidogrel at the Time of STEMI Fibrinolysis

Correct answer: Clopidogrel 300 mg loading, then 75 mg daily

Use the Reperfusion-Specific Regimen

**Clopidogrel is the recommended oral P2Y12 adjunct at fibrinolysis in the stated framework.** At age below seventy-five, use ==300 mg loading followed by 75 mg daily==.

The 2025 ACC/AHA narrative uses age at least seventy-five for the no-load 75 mg regimen, whereas its Table 7 uses older than seventy-five; ESC 2023 also uses older than seventy-five. Thus the exact seventy-fifth-year boundary is not internally consistent across these presentations. Follow the applicable local protocol at that boundary; this sixty-eight-year-old case is unambiguous and does not test the discrepancy.

Do not transfer a primary-PCI preference for another P2Y12 agent directly into the initial lysis prescription.

Complete and Reconcile Concomitant Treatment

**Aspirin and a suitable parenteral anticoagulant are also part of the pathway.** Select and dose the anticoagulant using age, weight and renal function.

For example, the cited enoxaparin lysis regimen below age seventy-five with adequate renal function begins with 30 mg IV, then 1 mg/kg subcutaneously every twelve hours, with the first two doses capped at 100 mg.

That example must not be copied to older patients or severe renal impairment without adjustment. Record all pretransfer doses and times so the receiving PCI team avoids duplication. Monitor for bleeding and assess reperfusion while arranging transfer. Later switching or procedural loading decisions depend on elapsed time, previous exposure and the invasive plan; the initial clopidogrel choice does not supply permission for an unplanned extra load of another agent.

Ticagrelor 180 mg loading, then 90 mg twice daily: Ticagrelor has an important role in ACS, particularly PCI pathways, but is not the recommended initial oral P2Y12 regimen given concurrently with fibrinolysis here.

Clopidogrel 75 mg daily without a loading dose: A no-loading regimen is used in older fibrinolysis patients; the sixty-eight-year-old in this question is clearly within the loading-dose group.

Prasugrel 60 mg loading, then 10 mg daily: Prasugrel is used in selected PCI-treated ACS patients after appropriate assessment, rather than as the standard P2Y12 adjunct at fibrinolytic administration.

ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI ACS guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009

ESC ACS guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad191

questions.question: A stable NSTE-ACS patient has unknown coronary anatomy and angiography planned in four hours. Under the 2023 ESC approach, which P2Y12 strategy is appropriate?
options: Defer routine oral P2Y12 loading until anatomy and the revascularization plan are known
Give prasugrel 60 mg now, before transfer to the catheterization laboratory
Give ticagrelor 180 mg now, before transfer to the catheterization laboratory
Give clopidogrel 600 mg now, before transfer to the catheterization laboratory
questions.explanation:
P2Y12 Pretreatment Before Early Angiography

Correct answer: Defer routine oral P2Y12 loading until anatomy and the revascularization plan are known

Define Pretreatment Precisely

**Pretreatment means giving a P2Y12 inhibitor before coronary anatomy is known.** It is a timing decision, not a decision to omit appropriate eventual antiplatelet treatment.

For planned early angiography within twenty-four hours in NSTE-ACS, the 2023 ESC guideline discourages routine pretreatment.

Aspirin and appropriate anticoagulation are separate treatment decisions and are not automatically deferred with the oral P2Y12 load.

Account for Delay and the Possible Treatment Path

**Anatomy may identify a surgical indication or another diagnosis**, so unnecessary early platelet inhibition can add harm without benefit.

If angiography will be substantially delayed, a different individualized pretreatment decision may be appropriate after assessing bleeding risk; the 2025 ACC/AHA guidance permits consideration of upstream clopidogrel or ticagrelor when the delay exceeds twenty-four hours.

Do not transfer the rule unchanged to STEMI or concurrent fibrinolysis. After anatomy is known, select the agent and timing according to PCI, surgery or medical management, comorbidity and contraindications. Record any doses already given during transfer so a deferred strategy does not become accidental duplicate loading when the patient reaches the catheterization laboratory.

Give prasugrel 60 mg now, before transfer to the catheterization laboratory: Prasugrel is effective for eligible PCI patients after the treatment decision, but pretreatment before anatomy is known failed to improve ischemic outcomes and increased bleeding in ACCOAST.

Give ticagrelor 180 mg now, before transfer to the catheterization laboratory: Ticagrelor is appropriate in eligible ACS treatment and may be considered upstream with substantially delayed angiography, but routine pretreatment is discouraged in this early-invasive unknown-anatomy setting.

Give clopidogrel 600 mg now, before transfer to the catheterization laboratory: Clopidogrel can be selected when potent agents are unsuitable or in other defined pathways, but its lower potency does not remove bleeding or surgical concerns that favor deferral here.

ESC ACS guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad191

ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI ACS guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009

questions.question: A patient with confirmed ACS can swallow and has no aspirin hypersensitivity or active bleeding. No loading dose has been given. Under the 2025 ACC/AHA guideline, which oral regimen is appropriate?
options: Aspirin 162–325 mg initially, followed by 325 mg daily as the preferred maintenance dose
Aspirin 75–100 mg initially, followed by 75–100 mg daily
Aspirin 162–325 mg initially, followed by 75–100 mg daily
Aspirin 75–100 mg initially, followed by 325 mg daily
questions.explanation:
Aspirin Loading and Maintenance in ACS

Correct answer: Aspirin 162–325 mg initially, followed by 75–100 mg daily

Separate Rapid Platelet Inhibition From Maintenance

**Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet cyclooxygenase-1 and thromboxane production.** The 2025 ACC/AHA ACS regimen is an oral load of ==162–325 mg== followed by ==75–100 mg daily==.

Use a nonenteric-coated preparation for prompt absorption; chewing the initial dose accelerates its effect when oral administration is suitable.

A history of low-dose aspirin use does not automatically remove the guideline loading recommendation. Confirm what was actually administered during transfer to prevent undocumented duplicate doses.

Integrate Aspirin With the Rest of ACS Treatment

**Aspirin and a P2Y12 inhibitor act at different platelet pathways.** The accompanying agent and treatment duration depend on reperfusion strategy, bleeding risk and other indications for anticoagulation.

Active pathological bleeding or a serious hypersensitivity history requires an alternative specialist plan. Gastrointestinal risk should prompt assessment and appropriate gastroprotection rather than indiscriminate high-dose maintenance.

Low-dose maintenance provides effective thromboxane suppression. Trials have not established superior clinical protection from maintaining the acute loading range, and some ACS comparisons showed more gastrointestinal or minor bleeding with higher doses. Reassess the regimen when bleeding occurs or oral anticoagulation is needed; the initial recommendation does not imply that aspirin must continue unchanged through every later combination strategy. Give clear discharge instructions distinguishing the loading dose already received from the ongoing daily dose.

Aspirin 162–325 mg initially, followed by 325 mg daily as the preferred maintenance dose: The initial loading range is appropriate, but prolonged full-dose aspirin is not the preferred maintenance strategy and adds bleeding burden without established superior ACS protection.

Aspirin 75–100 mg initially, followed by 75–100 mg daily: Low-dose aspirin is suitable maintenance treatment, but a larger initial loading dose is recommended to establish prompt platelet inhibition during ACS.

Aspirin 75–100 mg initially, followed by 325 mg daily: This reverses the intended loading and maintenance approach: the acute phase requires a loading dose, while subsequent treatment generally uses low-dose aspirin.

ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI ACS guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009

questions.question: A 62-year-old patient weighing 76 kg undergoes PCI for NSTEMI. There was an ischemic stroke five years earlier, without intracranial hemorrhage. Bleeding risk is not high, oral anticoagulation is unnecessary, and ticagrelor is tolerated and affordable. Which oral P2Y12 regimen is preferred among these choices?
options: Prasugrel 60 mg loading, then 10 mg daily
Ticagrelor 180 mg loading, then 90 mg twice daily
Clopidogrel 600 mg loading, then 75 mg daily
Ticagrelor 180 mg loading, then 60 mg twice daily
questions.explanation:
P2Y12 Selection After a Previous Ischemic Stroke

Correct answer: Ticagrelor 180 mg loading, then 90 mg twice daily

Distinguish Ischemic Stroke From Intracranial Hemorrhage

**Previous stroke or TIA excludes prasugrel**, irrespective of the reassuring age and weight in this vignette. Reducing the prasugrel dose does not remove that restriction.

A remote ischemic stroke is not the same contraindication as previous intracranial hemorrhage for ticagrelor. Review the actual diagnosis rather than accepting an unspecified history of stroke.

For an eligible ACS patient undergoing PCI, the 2025 ACC/AHA guideline favors ticagrelor or prasugrel over clopidogrel; the prior stroke directs selection away from prasugrel.

Prescribe and Monitor the Selected Agent

**The initial ACS ticagrelor regimen is a 180 mg load followed by 90 mg twice daily.** Check prior loading during transfer before prescribing another dose.

Monitor bleeding, dyspnea and clinically important bradyarrhythmia. Review strong CYP3A inhibitors or inducers and adherence to twice-daily treatment.

Active pathological bleeding or previous intracranial hemorrhage precludes ticagrelor. Clopidogrel remains useful when the balance of bleeding, tolerability, drug interactions, cost or concurrent anticoagulation favors it. Prasugrel additionally requires caution in older or low-weight patients: its age and weight dose considerations apply only after contraindications are excluded. Combine the selected agent with low-dose aspirin initially unless a specific alternative strategy is indicated, and reassess duration as ischemic and bleeding risks evolve. The question concerns the initial post-PCI choice, not a universal commitment to unchanged dual therapy indefinitely.

Prasugrel 60 mg loading, then 10 mg daily: This is a standard prasugrel regimen in appropriately selected PCI patients, but any previous stroke or TIA makes prasugrel unsuitable because of adverse net clinical outcomes.

Clopidogrel 600 mg loading, then 75 mg daily: Clopidogrel is a reasonable alternative when potent agents are unsuitable, bleeding risk is high or anticoagulation is required; the stated eligible PCI patient favors ticagrelor over clopidogrel.

Ticagrelor 180 mg loading, then 60 mg twice daily: The 60 mg twice-daily dose is used in selected extended secondary prevention settings after the first year; it is not the standard initial ACS maintenance dose.

ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI ACS guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009

    • Monitor bleeding, dyspnea and clinically important bradyarrhythmia. Review strong CYP3A inhibitors or inducers and adherence to twice-daily treatment.
    • Active pathological bleeding or previous intracranial hemorrhage precludes ticagrelor. Clopidogrel remains useful when the balance of bleeding, tolerability, drug interactions, cost or concurrent anticoagulation favors it. Prasugrel additionally requires caution in older or low-weight patients: its age and weight dose considerations apply only after contraindications are excluded. Combine the selected agent with low-dose aspirin initially unless a specific alternative strategy is indicated, and reassess duration as ischemic and bleeding risks evolve. The question concerns the initial post-PCI choice, not a universal commitment to unchanged dual therapy indefinitely.

Other Options

  • A — Prasugrel 60 mg loading, then 10 mg daily: This is a standard prasugrel regimen in appropriately selected PCI patients, but any previous stroke or TIA makes prasugrel unsuitable because of adverse net clinical outcomes.
  • C — Clopidogrel 600 mg loading, then 75 mg daily: Clopidogrel is a reasonable alternative when potent agents are unsuitable, bleeding risk is high or anticoagulation is required; the stated eligible PCI patient favors ticagrelor over clopidogrel.
  • D — Ticagrelor 180 mg loading, then 60 mg twice daily: The 60 mg twice-daily dose is used in selected extended secondary prevention settings after the first year; it is not the standard initial ACS maintenance dose.

questions.question: A 58-year-old, 82-kg patient with STEMI is proceeding directly to primary PCI without fibrinolysis. Prasugrel has been selected after contraindication screening. No P2Y12 inhibitor has been administered. Which regimen is appropriate?
options: Prasugrel 10 mg initially, followed by 10 mg daily
Prasugrel 60 mg loading, followed by 10 mg daily
Prasugrel 60 mg loading, followed by 5 mg daily
Prasugrel 30 mg loading, followed by 10 mg daily
questions.explanation:
Prasugrel Loading for Primary PCI

Correct answer: Prasugrel 60 mg loading, followed by 10 mg daily

Match the Regimen to the Reperfusion Strategy

**For eligible ACS patients undergoing PCI, prasugrel is loaded at 60 mg orally.** In a patient younger than seventy-five years and weighing at least sixty kilograms, the usual maintenance dose is ==10 mg daily==.

Exclude previous stroke or TIA and active pathological bleeding before prescribing. A contraindication cannot be corrected merely by reducing the dose.

Age at least seventy-five years or body weight below sixty kilograms requires separate caution and dose consideration; do not apply these adjustments to every patient.

Keep Primary PCI Distinct From Concurrent Fibrinolysis

**Prasugrel for primary PCI is not the standard oral adjunct administered with fibrinolysis.** Clopidogrel is used in the concurrent lytic pathway, with its own age-dependent loading approach.

Later PCI after fibrinolysis is a separate decision involving elapsed time, age, previous treatment and the selected guideline. Avoid treating a subsequent switch as permission to use any potent agent at the lytic bolus.

Check swallowing, absorption concerns and prior doses. Shock, vomiting or opioid exposure may delay oral drug effect; specialist intravenous antiplatelet treatment may be appropriate in selected circumstances. Continue bleeding surveillance and clear medication reconciliation through transfer. The choice among prasugrel, ticagrelor and clopidogrel depends on contraindications, reperfusion strategy and bleeding risk, while loading and maintenance are distinct prescribing steps. Do not mistake a correctly selected maintenance dose for adequate acute loading.

Prasugrel 10 mg initially, followed by 10 mg daily: Ten milligrams is the usual maintenance dose in this age and weight group; using it alone initially omits the loading dose needed for prompt platelet inhibition.

Prasugrel 60 mg loading, followed by 5 mg daily: Five-milligram maintenance is considered for low weight or older age with caution; neither dose-reduction feature is present in the stated patient.

Prasugrel 30 mg loading, followed by 10 mg daily: Thirty milligrams is not the standard guideline prasugrel loading regimen for this eligible primary-PCI presentation; it should not be inferred by halving another regimen.

ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI ACS guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009

questions.question: A 78-year-old patient receiving fibrinolysis for eligible STEMI weighs 70 kg and has a creatinine clearance of 24 mL/min. Enoxaparin is selected under its labeled STEMI regimen. Which initial schedule is appropriate?
options: No intravenous bolus; 70 mg subcutaneously every twelve hours
No intravenous bolus; 52.5 mg subcutaneously every twelve hours
A 30 mg intravenous bolus; 70 mg subcutaneously every twenty-four hours
No intravenous bolus; 70 mg subcutaneously every twenty-four hours
questions.explanation:
Enoxaparin When Age and Renal Adjustments Intersect

Correct answer: No intravenous bolus; 70 mg subcutaneously every twenty-four hours

Apply Both Adjustments to the Correct Indication

**The labeled STEMI regimen for age at least seventy-five years with creatinine clearance below thirty is 1 mg/kg subcutaneously once daily, without an intravenous bolus.** For seventy kilograms, this is ==70 mg every twenty-four hours==.

Without severe renal impairment, the older-patient STEMI regimen is 0.75 mg/kg every twelve hours without a bolus, with a seventy-five-milligram cap on each of the first two subcutaneous doses.

Do not simply combine the older-patient dose with the usual twelve-hour frequency when severe renal impairment is present. The renal table supplies the appropriate combined regimen.

Monitor Accumulation and Coordinate Subsequent Procedures

**Enoxaparin potentiates antithrombin-mediated factor Xa inhibition and has clinically important renal clearance.** Review weight, calculated creatinine clearance, blood count, platelets and bleeding before dosing.

Avoid using an indexed eGFR number interchangeably with the creatinine-clearance dosing criterion without assessing the patient and the estimation method.

Monitor changing renal function and overt or occult bleeding. Unfractionated heparin may be selected in some patients when rapid titration or reversibility is advantageous; that choice does not alter the labeled enoxaparin answer requested here. If PCI follows, document the exact last dose and time so procedural anticoagulation is selected safely. Prior heparin-induced thrombocytopenia or active major bleeding requires a different plan. Antiplatelet therapy and fibrinolytic age adjustments are separate decisions and must also be checked rather than inferred from the anticoagulant prescription.

STEMI fibrinolysis setting | Enoxaparin regimen | Initial qualification

Age <75; CrCl ≥30 mL/min | 30 mg IV, then 1 mg/kg SC every 12 h | First two SC doses maximum 100 mg each

Age ≥75; CrCl ≥30 mL/min | 0.75 mg/kg SC every 12 h | No IV bolus; first two SC doses maximum 75 mg each

Age <75; CrCl <30 mL/min: labeled STEMI regimen | 30 mg IV plus 1 mg/kg SC, then 1 mg/kg SC every 24 h | Renal adjustment changes SC frequency; initial IV bolus retained in this age group

Age ≥75; CrCl <30 mL/min | 1 mg/kg SC every 24 h | No IV bolus

UFH alternative: ACC/AHA 2025 | 60 units/kg IV then 12 units/kg/hour | Bolus maximum 4000 units; initial infusion maximum 1000 units/hour; adjust to therapeutic aPTT

No intravenous bolus; 70 mg subcutaneously every twelve hours: This preserves excessive dosing frequency for a creatinine clearance below thirty; omitting the bolus alone does not address renal accumulation.

No intravenous bolus; 52.5 mg subcutaneously every twelve hours: This applies the older-patient 0.75 mg/kg twice-daily regimen without making the additional severe-renal-impairment adjustment required at this creatinine clearance.

A 30 mg intravenous bolus; 70 mg subcutaneously every twenty-four hours: The once-daily renal adjustment is appropriate, but the initial intravenous bolus is omitted in STEMI patients at least seventy-five years old.

questions.question: A patient with NSTE-ACS received fondaparinux while awaiting delayed angiography. Renal function is adequate and there is no heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Angiography now identifies a lesion requiring PCI. Which anticoagulation step is appropriate?
options: Administer a procedural intravenous UFH bolus in addition to the prior fondaparinux
Proceed with fondaparinux as the sole procedural anticoagulant
Give an additional subcutaneous fondaparinux dose immediately before PCI
Start a ward-dose UFH infusion and postpone the procedural bolus until after PCI
questions.explanation:
PCI After Upstream Fondaparinux

Correct answer: Administer a procedural intravenous UFH bolus in addition to the prior fondaparinux

Recognize the Transition From Upstream Treatment to PCI

**Fondaparinux requires additional UFH when a treated NSTE-ACS patient proceeds to PCI.** The 2023 ESC guideline specifies a full-dose procedural bolus because guiding-catheter thrombosis is a concern.

Fondaparinux indirectly inhibits factor Xa through antithrombin. Its upstream efficacy does not establish that it can be used alone for every invasive procedure.

The principle is deliberate procedural supplementation, not indiscriminate switching among anticoagulants throughout admission.

Coordinate the Procedural Prescription

**Use the catheterization protocol and activated clotting-time assessment where appropriate.** Account for body weight, other anticoagulants, bleeding risk and planned glycoprotein IIb/IIIa use.

The FUTURA/OASIS-8 standard-dose strategy used UFH 85 units/kg, reduced to 60 units/kg with a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor; distinguish this trial protocol from a universal unqualified dose for all PCI situations.

Record the timing of prior fondaparinux and communicate it to the procedural team. Check renal function and contraindications before the upstream prescription and reassess if the clinical state changes. Antiplatelet treatment remains a separate component of PCI care. After an uncomplicated procedure, continued parenteral anticoagulation requires a specific indication rather than automatic continuation of every drug administered before catheterization. The key decision is to preserve appropriate upstream treatment while adding the anticoagulant coverage required for the invasive phase.

Proceed with fondaparinux as the sole procedural anticoagulant: Fondaparinux is useful upstream in selected NSTE-ACS patients, but alone it does not provide adequate catheter-related thrombotic protection during PCI.

Give an additional subcutaneous fondaparinux dose immediately before PCI: Repeating the upstream drug does not replace the recommended procedural UFH bolus and may increase bleeding without addressing the relevant procedural limitation.

Start a ward-dose UFH infusion and postpone the procedural bolus until after PCI: A UFH infusion is useful in selected upstream ACS pathways, but this patient now requires procedural anticoagulation; postponing the bolus leaves the catheterization phase inadequately covered.

ESC ACS guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad191

FUTURA/OASIS-8 randomized trial, 2010 — https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2010.1320

questions.question: A 76-year-old man undergoing ACS PCI has eGFR 45 mL/min/1.73 m², hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL and normal platelets. He has no prior bleeding, stroke, malignancy or anticoagulation indication. Which ARC-HBR interpretation is correct?
options: High bleeding risk is absent because three minor criteria are required
High bleeding risk is absent because no major criterion is present
High bleeding risk is present because moderate CKD is a major criterion
High bleeding risk is present because age and moderate CKD supply two minor criteria
questions.explanation:
Recognizing High Bleeding Risk Before PCI

Correct answer: High bleeding risk is present because age and moderate CKD supply two minor criteria

Apply the Binary Consensus Framework

**ARC-HBR requires at least one major or two minor criteria at PCI.** It is not an additive point score in which every item has equal weight.

Age at least 75 years and eGFR 30–59 each constitute a minor criterion. This patient has both, despite normal hemoglobin and no bleeding history.

The conceptual one-year boundaries are BARC 3 or 5 bleeding risk at least 4%, or intracranial hemorrhage risk at least 1%; they do not predict an exact individual event probability.

Translate Risk Into a Treatment Discussion

**High bleeding risk prompts individualized prevention of bleeding while preserving coronary protection.** It does not itself prohibit PCI or justify stopping both antiplatelets.

The 2025 ACS guideline allows selected abbreviated antiplatelet strategies; timing, retained agent and ischemic risk must be specified. Treat reversible anemia, avoid unnecessary NSAIDs and assess gastrointestinal protection when appropriate.

Recheck renal function and hemoglobin during follow-up. A patient may have both high ischemic and high bleeding risk, so neither label independently dictates the complete prescription.

Selected ARC-HBR feature | Minor criterion | Major criterion

Age | ≥75 years | Age alone does not supply a major criterion

Renal function | eGFR 30–59 mL/min/1.73 m² | eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m²

Hemoglobin | Men 11–12.9; women 11–11.9 g/dL | <11 g/dL

Baseline platelet count | No minor threshold in this framework | <100 × 10⁹/L

High bleeding risk is absent because three minor criteria are required: The consensus threshold is two minor criteria, not three; waiting for another abnormality would underrecognize this patient’s bleeding risk.

High bleeding risk is absent because no major criterion is present: One major criterion is sufficient but not necessary: two minor criteria also establish ARC-HBR, as in this combination of age and moderate CKD.

High bleeding risk is present because moderate CKD is a major criterion: An eGFR of 30–59 is a minor criterion; severe CKD below 30 supplies the major renal criterion, so this reaches the right label through the wrong classification.

sections.heading: Apply the Binary Consensus Framework

bullets.text: **ARC-HBR requires at least one major or two minor criteria at PCI.** It is not an additive point score in which every item has equal weight.
children: Age at least 75 years and eGFR 30–59 each constitute a minor criterion. This patient has both, despite normal hemoglobin and no bleeding history.
The conceptual one-year boundaries are BARC 3 or 5 bleeding risk at least 4%, or intracranial hemorrhage risk at least 1%; they do not predict an exact individual event probability.

sections.heading: Translate Risk Into a Treatment Discussion

bullets.text: **High bleeding risk prompts individualized prevention of bleeding while preserving coronary protection.** It does not itself prohibit PCI or justify stopping both antiplatelets.
children: The 2025 ACS guideline allows selected abbreviated antiplatelet strategies; timing, retained agent and ischemic risk must be specified. Treat reversible anemia, avoid unnecessary NSAIDs and assess gastrointestinal protection when appropriate.
Recheck renal function and hemoglobin during follow-up. A patient may have both high ischemic and high bleeding risk, so neither label independently dictates the complete prescription.

rows: Age alone does not supply a major criterion
No minor threshold in this framework

otherOptions.explanation: The consensus threshold is two minor criteria, not three; waiting for another abnormality would underrecognize this patient’s bleeding risk.
One major criterion is sufficient but not necessary: two minor criteria also establish ARC-HBR, as in this combination of age and moderate CKD.
An eGFR of 30–59 is a minor criterion; severe CKD below 30 supplies the major renal criterion, so this reaches the right label through the wrong classification.

questions.question: An ACS patient has undergone uncomplicated PCI and is preparing for discharge on aspirin plus ticagrelor. There is no high bleeding risk or oral anticoagulation indication. What is the default duration framework under the 2025 ACC/AHA guideline?
options: Plan six months of DAPT followed by aspirin alone
Plan one month of DAPT followed by aspirin alone
Plan at least twelve months of DAPT, with reassessment if the risk balance changes
Plan thirty-six months of DAPT from discharge
questions.explanation:
DAPT Duration After ACS Is a Risk-Based Prescription

Correct answer: Plan at least twelve months of DAPT, with reassessment if the risk balance changes

Begin With the ACS Default and Reassess

**The 2025 ACC/AHA default is aspirin plus an oral P2Y12 inhibitor for at least twelve months in ACS without high bleeding risk.** This addresses recurrent ischemic events as well as stent thrombosis.

Record bleeding history, anemia, renal dysfunction, concomitant drugs and anticipated procedures. Risk changes during follow-up, so the discharge plan needs explicit review.

A minimum default is not a command to continue both agents through major bleeding, nor proof that every patient benefits from extension beyond one year.

Distinguish Evidence-Based Bleeding Reduction Strategies

**Selected patients can transition to a different regimen without abandoning antiplatelet protection.** The agent retained and the timing matter.

For patients who have tolerated ticagrelor-based DAPT, the 2025 guideline supports ticagrelor monotherapy at least one month after PCI to reduce bleeding. This means withdrawing aspirin while continuing ticagrelor, not stopping both agents.

In high-bleeding-risk ACS PCI patients, single antiplatelet therapy after one month may be reasonable under the named framework. These strategies are not interchangeable with immediate aspirin withdrawal at the procedure, unguided early switching or a universal one-month course. Use a proton pump inhibitor when gastrointestinal bleeding risk warrants it. Explain adherence and the need to consult the treating team before interruption, especially early after stenting. A new anticoagulation indication requires its own combination strategy rather than simply adding another drug to unchanged DAPT.

Plan six months of DAPT followed by aspirin alone: Six-month courses apply in selected coronary contexts and individualized bleeding-risk strategies, but the named lower-bleeding-risk ACS default remains at least one year.

Plan one month of DAPT followed by aspirin alone: An abbreviated strategy can be appropriate in selected high-bleeding-risk patients, but it is not the default for this stated lower-bleeding-risk ACS presentation.

Plan thirty-six months of DAPT from discharge: Extended treatment can benefit selected prior-MI patients with favorable ischemic-to-bleeding balance, but it requires reassessment and is not the default duration for every ACS patient.

questions.question: A patient with atrial fibrillation requiring long-term anticoagulation has uncomplicated PCI for ACS. There is no mechanical valve, significant mitral stenosis or exceptionally high stent-thrombosis risk. Under the 2025 ACC/AHA framework, which planned sequence is preferred?
options: Continue anticoagulation, aspirin and clopidogrel together for twelve months
Brief triple therapy, then stop aspirin at one to four weeks and continue anticoagulation plus clopidogrel
Stop anticoagulation after PCI and use aspirin plus clopidogrel for twelve months
Stop clopidogrel at one week and continue anticoagulation plus aspirin
questions.explanation:
Antithrombotic Therapy When AF Coexists With ACS PCI

Correct answer: Brief triple therapy, then stop aspirin at one to four weeks and continue anticoagulation plus clopidogrel

Treat Two Thrombotic Indications With the Fewest Necessary Agents

**AF-related embolic prevention and post-PCI platelet inhibition have distinct indications.** Neither DAPT nor anticoagulation alone automatically supplies all early post-ACS protection.

The 2025 ACC/AHA guideline recommends stopping aspirin after ==one to four weeks== of triple therapy, continuing an oral anticoagulant plus a P2Y12 inhibitor, preferably clopidogrel.

Choose the exact aspirin stop date according to bleeding and stent-thrombosis risks. The stated uncomplicated case does not supply a reason for prolonged triple therapy.

Preserve Appropriate Anticoagulation and Follow-Up

**For eligible AF patients, a DOAC is generally preferred over a vitamin K antagonist.** Use the indicated stroke-prevention dose with its validated renal, age, weight and interaction adjustments.

Do not substitute the low vascular-prevention rivaroxaban dose for therapeutic AF anticoagulation. Mechanical valves and significant mitral stenosis require a separate anticoagulant assessment.

Reassess hemoglobin, renal function, adherence and gastrointestinal protection. Explain which drug stops and on what date: vague instructions to reduce blood thinners can cause the wrong agent to be withdrawn. The duration of subsequent anticoagulant-plus-clopidogrel treatment is individualized, commonly through the first post-ACS year, followed by reassessment for anticoagulant monotherapy. Recurrent ischemia, bleeding or repeat intervention can change that plan. Different society frameworks use somewhat different default early aspirin windows, so attribute the one-to-four-week interval to the named guideline rather than presenting it as an identical universal rule.

Continue anticoagulation, aspirin and clopidogrel together for twelve months: Prolonged triple therapy adds substantial bleeding risk; the usual strategy limits aspirin exposure while retaining anticoagulation and a P2Y12 inhibitor.

Stop anticoagulation after PCI and use aspirin plus clopidogrel for twelve months: DAPT protects against coronary events but does not replace indicated anticoagulation for AF-related cardioembolic stroke prevention.

Stop clopidogrel at one week and continue anticoagulation plus aspirin: The recommended early aspirin-withdrawal strategy retains a P2Y12 inhibitor, preferably clopidogrel; aspirin is not the usual agent retained in its place.

questions.question: Ten days after ACS stenting, a patient on aspirin and clopidogrel develops a major upper gastrointestinal bleed. Resuscitation is underway and endoscopic hemostasis is being arranged. Which antiplatelet principle is most appropriate?
options: Stop clopidogrel for two weeks while continuing aspirin and treating the bleeding source
Withhold both antiplatelets until a repeat endoscopy documents ulcer healing
Coordinate urgently with interventional cardiology, preserve aspirin if feasible, and minimize any necessary P2Y12 interruption
Stop aspirin permanently and continue clopidogrel alone as the immediate default
questions.explanation:
Major Gastrointestinal Bleeding Soon After Coronary Stenting

Correct answer: Coordinate urgently with interventional cardiology, preserve aspirin if feasible, and minimize any necessary P2Y12 interruption

Control Hemorrhage While Recognizing Very Early Stent Risk

**Resuscitation and source control proceed urgently.** Recent coronary stenting makes antiplatelet interruption hazardous, so involve the interventional cardiologist at the same time as the endoscopy team.

The BSG/ESGE 2021 framework favors continuing DAPT when possible in patients with coronary stents. If major hemorrhage requires P2Y12 interruption, continue aspirin if feasible.

This is not an instruction to continue every agent through uncontrolled life-threatening bleeding. Severity, hemostatic success and the coronary anatomy determine the immediate individualized plan.

Write an Explicit Restart and Prevention Plan

**If still indicated, reinstate the P2Y12 inhibitor within five days under the named guidance.** This is a maximum interruption framework, not a reason to wait five days after secure hemostasis when earlier resumption is appropriate.

Assess the endoscopic lesion, recurrent bleeding risk, hemoglobin trend and coronary risk with both teams. Use appropriate proton pump inhibitor treatment and address ulcer causes.

Record the last doses, the reason for interruption, which agent continues and the intended reassessment time. A temporary hold without a restart owner can become an unintended permanent withdrawal. Heparin bridging does not replace the antiplatelet mechanism needed for a recent stent. Once stabilized, review whether the longer-term regimen can be adjusted to reduce bleeding while maintaining coronary protection. The decision is a coordinated treatment sequence rather than choosing hemorrhage or thrombosis as the only relevant danger.

Stop clopidogrel for two weeks while continuing aspirin and treating the bleeding source: Preserving aspirin can be appropriate, but a predetermined two-week P2Y12 interruption is longer than the named guideline framework for a still-indicated recent-stent agent; plan early reassessment and reinstatement.

Withhold both antiplatelets until a repeat endoscopy documents ulcer healing: Temporary interruption may be necessary in uncontrolled life-threatening hemorrhage, but requiring complete ulcer healing before resumption creates excessive early stent risk; coordinate the shortest necessary interruption after source control.

Stop aspirin permanently and continue clopidogrel alone as the immediate default: P2Y12 monotherapy is used in selected planned post-PCI strategies, but this acute major-bleeding presentation ten days after stenting requires coordinated hemostasis and individualized interruption rather than automatic permanent aspirin withdrawal.

questions.question: An ACS patient has continuing ischemic discomfort, blood pressure 138/82 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Tadalafil was taken eighteen hours earlier. Which immediate supportive-treatment plan is appropriate while definitive ACS care proceeds?
options: Give sublingual nitroglycerin because the current blood pressure is normal
Withhold nitrates and reassess pain and perfusion while expediting indicated coronary treatment
Use intravenous nitroglycerin because titration avoids the oral drug interaction
Give high-flow oxygen as the principal anti-ischemic treatment at the stated saturation
questions.explanation:
Recent Tadalafil Exposure During ACS

Correct answer: Withhold nitrates and reassess pain and perfusion while expediting indicated coronary treatment

Screen for Vasodilator Interactions Before Giving Nitrates

**Nitrates increase cyclic GMP, while PDE5 inhibition reduces its breakdown.** Combined exposure can produce profound hypotension despite an initially reassuring blood pressure.

The 2025 ACC/AHA ACS framework avoids nitrates within ==forty-eight hours of tadalafil==, twenty-four hours of sildenafil or vardenafil, and twelve hours of avanafil.

Also assess suspected right ventricular infarction, systolic pressure below ninety or a fall greater than thirty millimeters of mercury from baseline. Nitrate eligibility requires more than the absence of one contraindication.

Treat Persistent Ischemia Without Relying on Symptom Suppression

**Continuing ischemic discomfort requires reassessment of ECG, hemodynamics and the invasive or reperfusion plan.** Analgesia must not delay treatment of the cause.

At oxygen saturation below ninety percent, give oxygen to correct hypoxemia; routine supplemental oxygen is not recommended for the normally saturated patient described here.

Opioids may be considered selectively for severe pain unresponsive to other suitable measures, but can cause hypotension, respiratory depression and delayed absorption of oral P2Y12 drugs. Relief of pain does not prove reperfusion. When nitrates are otherwise suitable, sublingual nitroglycerin is commonly 0.3–0.4 mg every five minutes for up to three doses, with monitoring and further treatment based on response. Those usual doses remain inappropriate during the tadalafil interaction window. Record the drug and time of exposure explicitly so another clinician does not inadvertently administer a nitrate during transfer.

Give sublingual nitroglycerin because the current blood pressure is normal: Normal baseline pressure does not remove the nitrate–PDE5 inhibitor interaction; tadalafil exposure within forty-eight hours makes nitrate-associated hypotension a serious concern.

Use intravenous nitroglycerin because titration avoids the oral drug interaction: The interaction is pharmacodynamic and persists with intravenous nitrate delivery; changing the route does not remove excessive cyclic-GMP-mediated vasodilation.

Give high-flow oxygen as the principal anti-ischemic treatment at the stated saturation: Supplemental oxygen treats hypoxemia, but routine use at this normal saturation has no established benefit and does not substitute for addressing continuing coronary ischemia.

ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI ACS guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009

questions.question: After anterior MI, a patient has heart rate 112/min, blood pressure 92/64 mm Hg, cool extremities and pulmonary congestion. No beta blocker has been administered. Which approach is appropriate?
options: Give intravenous metoprolol promptly to correct the tachycardia
Defer beta-blocker initiation, treat the unstable state, and reassess after stabilization
Start low-dose oral metoprolol now with close blood-pressure monitoring
Start carvedilol now to obtain its longer-term ventricular-remodeling benefit
questions.explanation:
Defer Early Beta Blockade During Low Output

Correct answer: Defer beta-blocker initiation, treat the unstable state, and reassess after stabilization

Recognize Compensatory Tachycardia and Shock Risk

**Acute heart failure and low-output features are reasons to defer initiation of beta blockade.** A fast pulse does not establish that reducing it immediately will improve cardiac output.

Assess perfusion, congestion, ventricular function, ongoing ischemia and mechanical complications. Provide appropriate stabilization and coronary treatment.

Negative inotropy and reduced chronotropic support can worsen an already compromised circulation. Intravenous dosing does not bypass this physiological risk.

Reassess Eligibility After the Acute Contraindication Resolves

**The 2025 ACC/AHA guideline recommends early oral beta blockers in ACS without contraindications.** Begin at a low dose with cautious titration when blood pressure, perfusion and heart rate permit.

questions.question: Six weeks after ACS, a patient taking maximally tolerated atorvastatin 80 mg daily has LDL-C 86 mg/dL with confirmed adherence. Triglycerides are 130 mg/dL. Under the 2025 ACC/AHA ACS framework, which next step is appropriate?
options: Add a fibrate as the preferred response to the residual LDL elevation
Continue the same regimen because LDL-C is already below 100 mg/dL
Replace atorvastatin with a moderate-intensity statin before considering combination therapy
Add an evidence-based nonstatin LDL-lowering agent while continuing the tolerated statin
questions.explanation:
Nonstatin Escalation After ACS

Correct answer: Add an evidence-based nonstatin LDL-lowering agent while continuing the tolerated statin

Use the Named Guideline’s Escalation Threshold

**The 2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline recommends adding a nonstatin when LDL-C remains at least seventy mg/dL on maximally tolerated statin therapy.** At fifty-five to sixty-nine, addition is reasonable.

High-intensity statin treatment remains the foundation when tolerated. A numerically improved LDL does not establish that residual risk has been adequately addressed.

Reassess adherence, drug access, interactions and secondary causes before labeling treatment failure. The six-week measurement is within the recommended four-to-eight-week follow-up interval.

Select Additional Therapy According to Required Reduction

**Ezetimibe and PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies are established options with cardiovascular outcome evidence.** Selection depends on the magnitude of lowering needed, prior therapy, tolerance and access.

Ezetimibe is commonly prescribed at ten milligrams daily. A PCSK9 antibody can provide a larger additional reduction when the remaining LDL burden warrants it.

Distinguish an escalation threshold from a treatment goal. The 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline recommends LDL-C below 55 mg/dL and non-HDL-C below 85 mg/dL for very-high-risk secondary prevention; ASCVD patients outside that category generally have an LDL-C goal below 70 mg/dL, with further intensification toward below 55 reasonable in selected patients. Continue lifestyle treatment and reassess response. Avoid reducing a tolerated statin merely because combination treatment achieves a low LDL. Explain the additional agent and arrange a documented follow-up lipid measurement.

ACC/AHA ACS 2025 | LDL-C ≥70 mg/dL on maximal tolerated statin | Add a nonstatin

ACC/AHA ACS 2025 | LDL-C 55–69 mg/dL on maximal tolerated statin | Nonstatin addition is reasonable

ACC/AHA dyslipidemia 2026: very-high-risk ASCVD | LDL-C <55; non-HDL-C <85 mg/dL | Secondary-prevention treatment goals

ACC/AHA ACS 2025 | 4–8 weeks | Reassess lipid profile after discharge

ESC ACS 2023 | LDL-C <55 mg/dL and ≥50% reduction from baseline | Post-ACS treatment goals

ESC ACS 2023 | 4–6 weeks after treatment adjustment | Reassess response; add ezetimibe then PCSK9 inhibitor if goals remain unmet

Add a fibrate as the preferred response to the residual LDL elevation: Fibrates have selected triglyceride-related uses, but the stated normal triglycerides and residual LDL burden favor an LDL-directed outcome-supported nonstatin.

Continue the same regimen because LDL-C is already below 100 mg/dL: A threshold of one hundred does not reflect the named post-ACS escalation framework; LDL-C at least seventy on maximal statin treatment supports adding a nonstatin.

Replace atorvastatin with a moderate-intensity statin before considering combination therapy: Dose reduction is appropriate for intolerance or another specific reason, but the patient tolerates high-intensity treatment and needs additional LDL lowering.

questions.question: A clinician reviews contemporary randomized evidence for routine long-term beta blockers after an uncomplicated MI in patients with LVEF at least 50% and no other beta-blocker indication. Which interpretation is best supported by the 2025 individual-patient meta-analysis?
options: The findings support avoiding beta blockers during the acute admission as well as follow-up
Routine treatment established a mortality benefit equivalent to that in reduced-EF heart failure
Routine treatment did not reduce the composite of death, MI or heart failure in the preserved-EF population studied
The findings establish noninferiority of withdrawal in patients already receiving long-term treatment
questions.explanation:
Long-Term Beta Blockers With Preserved EF

Correct answer: Routine treatment did not reduce the composite of death, MI or heart failure in the preserved-EF population studied

Specify the EF Group and Clinical Question

**The 2025 individual-patient meta-analysis pooled contemporary trials in post-MI patients with LVEF at least fifty percent.** Routine beta blockers did not lower the composite of all-cause death, MI or heart failure.

This result should not be extended unchanged to EF forty to forty-nine percent, established HF, symptomatic angina, arrhythmia or another independent indication.

Distinguish long-term event prevention from the acute hemodynamic and antiarrhythmic decisions made during the infarct admission.

Separate Treatment Initiation From Withdrawal

**ABYSS studied interruption versus continuation in patients already receiving long-term beta blockers.** Failure to demonstrate noninferiority of interruption prevents a blanket claim that withdrawal is equivalent.

Trials differ in EF entry criteria, endpoints and time since MI. A broad statement that all modern trials prove the same result obscures those clinically important differences.

Review ventricular function, blood pressure, angina, rhythm, adverse effects and the original indication before changing an established prescription. If discontinuation is selected, use a supervised taper rather than an automatic abrupt stop. Continue proven secondary prevention irrespective of the beta-blocker decision. Explain that absence of demonstrated routine benefit in one population is not evidence that the drug has no role in coronary care. The appropriate conclusion is indication-based prescribing informed by the patient’s EF and clinical context, with separate attention to the risks of changing established treatment.

The findings support avoiding beta blockers during the acute admission as well as follow-up: The analysis concerns long-term treatment in a selected EF population, not an instruction to abandon acute use when indicated or treatment for another condition.

Routine treatment established a mortality benefit equivalent to that in reduced-EF heart failure: Benefit in reduced-EF HF cannot be transferred to normal-EF post-MI patients; the contemporary pooled preserved-EF evidence did not demonstrate that claimed benefit.

The findings establish noninferiority of withdrawal in patients already receiving long-term treatment: Initiation-versus-no-treatment evidence does not establish universal withdrawal safety; ABYSS addressed interruption separately and did not demonstrate noninferiority of interruption.

questions.question: A patient with ACS has hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL without active bleeding. The team is reviewing the 2025 ACC/AHA recommendation and MINT evidence. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: The nonsignificant MINT result establishes equivalent safety of restrictive and liberal strategies
A seven-gram threshold remains the preferred ACS default because restrictive trials in other inpatients apply directly
MINT proved a statistically significant reduction in its primary endpoint with liberal transfusion
A liberal transfusion strategy toward hemoglobin around ten may be reasonable, with individualized benefit–risk assessment
questions.explanation:
Transfusion Strategy in ACS With Anemia

Correct answer: A liberal transfusion strategy toward hemoglobin around ten may be reasonable, with individualized benefit–risk assessment

Read the Trial Result Without Converting Uncertainty Into Equivalence

**MINT compared restrictive and liberal transfusion strategies in MI with hemoglobin below ten.** Thirty-day death or MI occurred in 16.9% versus 14.5%, respectively.

The modeled relative risk for restrictive versus liberal treatment was 1.15, with a ninety-five-percent confidence interval of 0.99–1.34 and P=0.07.

This did not establish statistical superiority of the liberal strategy, but clinically important harm from a restrictive strategy could not be excluded. A nonsignificant result does not prove the strategies equivalent.

Apply the Recommendation to the Actual Patient

**The 2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline states that transfusion to achieve hemoglobin at least ten may be reasonable in ACS with anemia.** This is a qualified recommendation rather than a universal mandate.

Consider continuing ischemia, symptoms, anemia trajectory, heart failure, renal function and transfusion-associated circulatory overload. Reassess after each transfusion step according to clinical practice.

Investigate the cause of anemia and distinguish this nonbleeding presentation from active major hemorrhage, where resuscitation and source control have their own urgency. Review antithrombotic exposure and occult blood loss. Do not replace the measured clinical course with a single threshold detached from context, and do not extrapolate these ACS findings to every stable medical inpatient. Explain the expected benefit and uncertainty while monitoring for adverse transfusion effects. The question tests appropriate interpretation and individualized management, not certainty that one hemoglobin target is optimal for every patient.

The nonsignificant MINT result establishes equivalent safety of restrictive and liberal strategies: A superiority comparison with P=0.07 does not establish equivalence; its confidence interval still permits clinically important harm from the restrictive strategy.

A seven-gram threshold remains the preferred ACS default because restrictive trials in other inpatients apply directly: Restrictive thresholds are supported in several other settings, but ACS-specific evidence and the named recommendation warrant separate interpretation rather than direct extrapolation.

MINT proved a statistically significant reduction in its primary endpoint with liberal transfusion: The primary comparison favored liberal treatment numerically but did not reach conventional statistical significance; overstating certainty misrepresents the trial.

questions.question: A patient with chronic angina is taking diltiazem. Ranolazine extended release is being considered after review of renal function, ECG and other drugs. Under the US prescribing information, what is the maximum ranolazine dose while diltiazem continues?
options: 500 mg twice daily
1000 mg twice daily
750 mg twice daily
375 mg twice daily
questions.explanation:
Ranolazine With Concurrent Diltiazem

Correct answer: 500 mg twice daily

Identify the Pharmacokinetic Interaction

**Diltiazem is a moderate CYP3A inhibitor and increases ranolazine exposure.** The US prescribing information limits ranolazine to ==500 mg twice daily== during this combination.

The ordinary extended-release regimen starts at five hundred milligrams twice daily and may increase to one thousand twice daily when suitable; the interacting-drug limit overrides that usual ceiling.

Strong CYP3A inhibitors and CYP3A inducers are contraindicated combinations rather than situations managed simply by the same dose cap.

Screen Beyond Heart Rate and Blood Pressure

**Ranolazine inhibits late inward sodium current and can improve angina with relatively little effect on resting pulse or pressure.** Hemodynamic neutrality does not imply freedom from important adverse effects.

It can prolong QT in an exposure-dependent manner. Review baseline QT, other QT-prolonging medicines, electrolytes, renal function and liver disease; liver cirrhosis is a labeled contraindication.

Dizziness, constipation and nausea can limit treatment. Monitor renal function, particularly with impairment or an acute illness, and review interactions involving other substrates as well as inhibitors. Extended-release tablets should be taken according to the formulation instructions rather than crushed or converted into an improvised dosing schedule. The drug treats chronic symptoms and does not replace acute reperfusion, antiplatelet treatment or lipid lowering when those are indicated. If angina remains limiting at the safe tolerated dose, reassess the regimen and coronary mechanism rather than exceeding an interaction-based ceiling.

1000 mg twice daily: This is the usual maximum without a relevant interacting inhibitor, but diltiazem increases ranolazine exposure and lowers the permitted maximum.

750 mg twice daily: Seven hundred fifty milligrams twice daily is a usual maximum in some European product information, but the question specifies the US prescribing information and its diltiazem interaction ceiling.

375 mg twice daily: Three hundred seventy-five milligrams twice daily is a starting dose in some European formulations; it is not the specified US maximum during moderate CYP3A inhibition.

questions.explanationHtml:
Ranolazine With Concurrent Diltiazem

Correct answer: A — 500 mg twice daily

Identify the Pharmacokinetic Interaction

  • Diltiazem is a moderate CYP3A inhibitor and increases ranolazine exposure. The US prescribing information limits ranolazine to 500 mg twice daily during this combination.
    • The ordinary extended-release regimen starts at five hundred milligrams twice daily and may increase to one thousand twice daily when suitable; the interacting-drug limit overrides that usual ceiling.
    • Strong CYP3A inhibitors and CYP3A inducers are contraindicated combinations rather than situations managed simply by the same dose cap.

Screen Beyond Heart Rate and Blood Pressure

  • Ranolazine inhibits late inward sodium current and can improve angina with relatively little effect on resting pulse or pressure. Hemodynamic neutrality does not imply freedom from important adverse effects.
    • It can prolong QT in an exposure-dependent manner. Review baseline QT, other QT-prolonging medicines, electrolytes, renal function and liver disease; liver cirrhosis is a labeled contraindication.
    • Dizziness, constipation and nausea can limit treatment. Monitor renal function, particularly with impairment or an acute illness, and review interactions involving other substrates as well as inhibitors. Extended-release tablets should be taken according to the formulation instructions rather than crushed or converted into an improvised dosing schedule. The drug treats chronic symptoms and does not replace acute reperfusion, antiplatelet treatment or lipid lowering when those are indicated. If angina remains limiting at the safe tolerated dose, reassess the regimen and coronary mechanism rather than exceeding an interaction-based ceiling.

Other Options

  • B — 1000 mg twice daily: This is the usual maximum without a relevant interacting inhibitor, but diltiazem increases ranolazine exposure and lowers the permitted maximum.
  • C — 750 mg twice daily: Seven hundred fifty milligrams twice daily is a usual maximum in some European product information, but the question specifies the US prescribing information and its diltiazem interaction ceiling.
  • D — 375 mg twice daily: Three hundred seventy-five milligrams twice daily is a starting dose in some European formulations; it is not the specified US maximum during moderate CYP3A inhibition.

References

  • Ranolazine extended-release prescribing information
  • Ranexa UK Summary of Product Characteristics
  • ESC chronic coronary syndromes guideline, 2024

questions.topic: Chronic coronary disease angina and landmark evidence
questions.question: A stable patient has a seventy-percent unprotected left-main stenosis. A colleague cites ISCHEMIA as proof that an initial conservative strategy is equivalent for this anatomy. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Significant unprotected left-main disease was excluded, so the trial cannot justify that extrapolation
The overall neutral comparison supports medical therapy first for this left-main lesion
The conservative arm prohibited later angiography, limiting comparison with current practice
The lack of statistical significance establishes equivalence between strategies in stable CAD
questions.explanation:
Applying ISCHEMIA Beyond Its Enrollment Population

Correct answer: Significant unprotected left-main disease was excluded, so the trial cannot justify that extrapolation

Check Eligibility Before Applying a Trial Result

**ISCHEMIA enrolled selected stable patients with moderate or severe ischemia.** Significant unprotected left-main disease was excluded, so its initial-strategy comparison does not settle management of this patient.

Other major exclusions included EF below thirty-five percent, recent ACS, unacceptable angina despite maximally tolerated treatment and advanced kidney disease in the main trial.

The parallel ISCHEMIA-CKD study addressed a different kidney-disease population and must not be silently substituted for the main trial.

Distinguish Strategy, Symptoms and Prognosis

**An initial conservative strategy includes active medical treatment and later angiography when indicated.** It does not mean permanent prohibition of revascularization.

The November 2026 ISCHEMIA-EXTEND report found no significant all-cause survival difference over a median nine-year follow-up. Estimated eleven-year mortality was 25.8% with initial invasion versus 26.9% with initial conservative management; adjusted hazard ratio 0.97, ninety-five-percent confidence interval 0.86–1.09. This survival analysis does not eliminate symptom benefits or extend eligibility to excluded patients.

Significant left-main disease requires anatomy-based specialist assessment and consideration of revascularization, often through a Heart Team. The suitable method depends on complexity, operative risk and other patient factors. Do not use a nonsignificant overall trial comparison to claim formal equivalence in an excluded subgroup. Similarly, severe uncontrolled symptoms remain a clinical indication for reassessment even when a patient otherwise resembles trial participants. The central examination skill is external validity: identify who was randomized, which strategies were compared and which conclusion the data can actually support.

The overall neutral comparison supports medical therapy first for this left-main lesion: An overall result applies within the population and strategies studied; it cannot establish a conservative-first conclusion for significant left-main disease that the trial excluded.

The conservative arm prohibited later angiography, limiting comparison with current practice: The conservative strategy allowed angiography and revascularization for clinical indications; the relevant limitation here is excluded anatomy rather than a permanent ban on invasive care.

The lack of statistical significance establishes equivalence between strategies in stable CAD: Failure to demonstrate superiority does not establish formal equivalence, and neither interpretation can extend the randomized comparison to this excluded anatomical subgroup.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the original FAME and COURAGE randomized trials?
options: FAME compared FFR-selected PCI with medical therapy; COURAGE compared PCI with CABG
FAME compared PCI with medical therapy alone; COURAGE compared physiological with angiographic PCI guidance
FAME compared physiological versus angiographic PCI guidance; COURAGE compared initial PCI plus medical therapy with medical therapy alone
FAME compared FFR-guided with angiographic PCI; COURAGE compared intensive with moderate lipid lowering
questions.explanation:
FAME and COURAGE Answer Different Questions

Correct answer: FAME compared physiological versus angiographic PCI guidance; COURAGE compared initial PCI plus medical therapy with medical therapy alone

Identify the Randomized Comparison

**Original FAME tested FFR-guided versus angiography-guided multivessel PCI.** In the physiological arm, lesions were treated when FFR was at most 0.80.

At one year, the composite of death, MI or repeat revascularization was 13.2% with FFR guidance versus 18.3% with angiographic guidance. This is a composite strategy result, not proof of isolated mortality benefit.

Do not confuse original FAME with FAME 2, which addressed a different comparison involving FFR-selected PCI and medical therapy.

Interpret Medical-Therapy Evidence Without Abandoning Symptom Care

**COURAGE compared initial PCI plus optimal medical therapy with optimal medical therapy alone in selected stable coronary disease.** It did not demonstrate a reduction in death or nonfatal MI from adding initial PCI.

Medical therapy in both arms was active preventive and antianginal treatment. A conservative initial strategy did not prohibit later revascularization when clinically required.

FFR reflects the pressure consequence of an epicardial lesion during hyperemia; it is not a test that excludes every microvascular or vasospastic mechanism of angina. Interpret borderline measurements and acute-infarct physiology with appropriate clinical caution. Use the trials to clarify whether a patient needs revascularization and, separately, which lesions should be treated. Their results do not negate symptom-directed intervention or anatomy-specific prognostic indications outside the studied comparison. Knowing the trial name is less useful than identifying its population, comparator and endpoint.

FAME compared FFR-selected PCI with medical therapy; COURAGE compared PCI with CABG: The first comparison resembles FAME 2 rather than original FAME; COURAGE compared adding PCI to medical therapy and did not randomize patients between PCI and CABG.

FAME compared PCI with medical therapy alone; COURAGE compared physiological with angiographic PCI guidance: These trial designs are reversed: original FAME studied how to select lesions during planned multivessel PCI, whereas COURAGE studied adding initial PCI to medical therapy.

FAME compared FFR-guided with angiographic PCI; COURAGE compared intensive with moderate lipid lowering: The FAME description is correct, but COURAGE randomized the initial PCI strategy on a background of optimal medical therapy, not statin intensity as its assigned intervention.

COURAGE randomized trial, 2007 — https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa070829

FAME randomized trial, 2009 — https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa0807611

AHA/ACC chronic coronary disease guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2023.04.003

questions.topic: Chronic coronary disease angina and landmark evidence
questions.question: A patient with stable coronary and peripheral arterial disease has high recurrent ischemic risk, low bleeding risk, adequate renal function and no indication for DAPT or therapeutic anticoagulation. Which regimen is an evidence-supported option for intensifying long-term prevention?
options: Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus low-dose aspirin
Rivaroxaban 20 mg daily plus low-dose aspirin
Rivaroxaban 5 mg twice daily without aspirin
Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus clopidogrel
questions.explanation:
Selected Long-Term Dual-Pathway Inhibition

Correct answer: Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus low-dose aspirin

Select Patients Before Intensifying Antithrombotic Treatment

**Low-dose rivaroxaban plus aspirin is an option in selected high-ischemic-risk chronic coronary disease without high bleeding risk.** The 2023 AHA/ACC framework specifies no separate need for therapeutic DOAC dosing or DAPT.

The vascular dose is ==2.5 mg twice daily== with low-dose aspirin. It must not be substituted for therapeutic anticoagulation when AF or venous thromboembolism requires it.

Review bleeding history, renal and hepatic function, stroke history, interactions and adherence. Polyvascular disease increases ischemic risk but does not erase bleeding contraindications.

Explain the COMPASS Benefit and Harm Together

**COMPASS showed fewer cardiovascular deaths, strokes or MIs with the combination than with aspirin alone.** Primary events occurred in 4.1% versus 5.4%, with hazard ratio 0.76.

Major bleeding increased: 3.1% versus 1.9%, with hazard ratio 1.70. The result supports patient selection rather than universal intensification.

Continue lipid lowering, smoking cessation, blood-pressure management and exercise-based care; antithrombotic escalation does not replace these interventions. Reassess the regimen if bleeding, renal deterioration or a new anticoagulation indication develops. Extended DAPT in selected prior-MI patients is a different strategy with its own evidence and eligibility, not a reason to combine every available agent. Discuss both expected ischemic benefit and bleeding burden so the chosen prescription reflects the individual patient’s risk and preferences.

Rivaroxaban 20 mg daily plus low-dose aspirin: Therapeutic-dose rivaroxaban has other indications such as eligible AF stroke prevention; it is not the COMPASS low-dose combination strategy requested here.

Rivaroxaban 5 mg twice daily without aspirin: This rivaroxaban-alone arm was studied in COMPASS but did not establish the same benefit as low-dose rivaroxaban plus aspirin; the successful combination cannot be replaced by this higher-dose monotherapy.

Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus clopidogrel: Clopidogrel is appropriate in several coronary and peripheral-arterial contexts, but substituting it for aspirin does not reproduce the COMPASS randomized combination evidence tested by this question.

COMPASS randomized trial, 2017 — https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1709118

AHA/ACC chronic coronary disease guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2023.04.003

questions.question: Which interpretation of the EARLY TAVR randomized trial is most accurate when discussing intervention with an asymptomatic older patient with severe aortic stenosis and preserved EF?
options: Early TAVR reduced the composite of death, stroke or unplanned cardiovascular hospitalization compared with surveillance
Early TAVR established an isolated all-cause mortality benefit as its primary finding
The comparison established TAVR superiority over surgical valve replacement
The comparison established benefit of TAVR in moderate aortic stenosis with reduced EF
questions.explanation:
Interpreting EARLY TAVR Without Overstating Mortality Benefit

Correct answer: Early TAVR reduced the composite of death, stroke or unplanned cardiovascular hospitalization compared with surveillance

Population, Comparator and Endpoint

**EARLY TAVR randomized 901 patients with asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis to early TAVR or clinical surveillance.** It addressed timing of intervention, not a direct comparison with surgery.

The primary composite occurred in 26.8% versus 45.3%, hazard ratio 0.50 with 95% confidence interval 0.40–0.63. Interpretation must retain the endpoint components.

Unplanned cardiovascular hospitalization occurred in 20.9% versus 41.7%; stroke in 4.2% versus 6.7%; death in 8.4% versus 9.2%. These component figures should not be presented as if each independently established the same statistical conclusion.

Clinical Application

**An early-intervention discussion should consider trial eligibility and lifetime treatment consequences.** Asymptomatic status, stenosis severity, ventricular function, anatomy and procedural suitability matter.

Clinical surveillance is active care with symptom education, repeat assessment and later intervention when indicated. It is not permanent refusal of replacement.

The findings support reconsidering timing in appropriate severe disease, while leaving procedure selection to individualized Heart Team assessment. They do not establish benefit in every younger patient, every anatomy or every less-than-severe lesion. Explain potential procedural harms and later prosthesis-related decisions alongside the composite benefit. A qualified discussion is more useful than converting a trial result into a universal instruction to implant immediately.

Early TAVR established an isolated all-cause mortality benefit as its primary finding: The primary endpoint was a composite. Death occurred in 8.4% versus 9.2%; the significant composite result cannot be relabeled as a demonstrated isolated mortality benefit.

The comparison established TAVR superiority over surgical valve replacement: The randomized comparator was clinical surveillance, not surgery; the trial does not directly determine which replacement approach is superior.

The comparison established benefit of TAVR in moderate aortic stenosis with reduced EF: This is a different disease-severity and ventricular-function question; EARLY TAVR studied asymptomatic severe disease rather than that moderate-AS population.

EARLY TAVR randomized trial, 2024 online/2025 print — https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2405880

ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf194

children: The primary composite occurred in 26.8% versus 45.3%, hazard ratio 0.50 with 95% confidence interval 0.40–0.63. Interpretation must retain the endpoint components.

Unplanned cardiovascular hospitalization occurred in 20.9% versus 41.7%; stroke in 4.2% versus 6.7%; death in 8.4% versus 9.2%. These component figures should not be presented as if each independently established the same statistical conclusion.

sections.heading: Clinical Application

bullets.text: **An early-intervention discussion should consider trial eligibility and lifetime treatment consequences.** Asymptomatic status, stenosis severity, ventricular function, anatomy and procedural suitability matter.
children: Clinical surveillance is active care with symptom education, repeat assessment and later intervention when indicated. It is not permanent refusal of replacement.

The findings support reconsidering timing in appropriate severe disease, while leaving procedure selection to individualized Heart Team assessment. They do not establish benefit in every younger patient, every anatomy or every less-than-severe lesion. Explain potential procedural harms and later prosthesis-related decisions alongside the composite benefit. A qualified discussion is more useful than converting a trial result into a universal instruction to implant immediately.

The randomized comparator was clinical surveillance, not surgery; the trial does not directly determine which replacement approach is superior.

questions.question: A nonpregnant adult with rheumatic mitral stenosis, valve area 1.1 cm² and persistent AF needs long-term embolic prevention. There is no active bleeding and INR monitoring is feasible. Which strategy is best supported?
options: Rivaroxaban at the standard renal-adjusted AF dose
A vitamin K antagonist adjusted to INR 2–3
Apixaban at the standard age-, weight- and renal-adjusted AF dose
Aspirin plus clopidogrel instead of oral anticoagulation
questions.explanation:
Anticoagulant Selection in Rheumatic MS With AF

Correct answer: A vitamin K antagonist adjusted to INR 2–3

Valve-Specific Thromboembolic Risk

**Rheumatic mitral obstruction and AF promote atrial stasis and thrombus formation.** Anticoagulant selection must incorporate the valve lesion rather than rely only on a general AF risk score.

The ESC 2025 MS section specifies VKA therapy with INR 2–3 for AF and advises avoiding DOACs with mitral valve area ≤2.0 cm² on current evidence. This case is well within the clinically important rheumatic range.

Review bleeding, interactions, renal and hepatic disease, adherence and monitoring access. A fixed warfarin dose cannot replace INR-guided adjustment.

Randomized Evidence and Monitoring

**INVICTUS compared rivaroxaban with adjusted VKA therapy in rheumatic heart disease-associated AF.** VKA produced fewer primary composite events without a significant increase in major bleeding.

The composite included stroke, systemic embolism, MI and death from vascular or unknown causes. Its interpretation must retain that population and endpoint.

Explain INR testing, dose changes, interactions and consistency of vitamin K intake. Investigate inadequate time in therapeutic range and address barriers rather than assuming any DOAC is an evidence-equivalent substitute. Rate control, rhythm management and relief of valve obstruction are separate decisions; none automatically removes an ongoing anticoagulation indication. Pregnancy requires a dedicated maternal–fetal anticoagulation plan and should not be managed by copying this nonpregnant prescription.

Rivaroxaban at the standard renal-adjusted AF dose: Standard AF dosing does not overcome the evidence limitation in rheumatic MS; INVICTUS favored VKA over rivaroxaban for its primary composite outcome.

Apixaban at the standard age-, weight- and renal-adjusted AF dose: Apixaban is appropriate for many AF patients, but the general DOAC preference should not be transferred to clinically important rheumatic MS, which requires the established VKA strategy.

Aspirin plus clopidogrel instead of oral anticoagulation: Dual antiplatelet therapy has coronary indications but does not provide equivalent prevention of atrial cardioembolic events in this high-risk valve-associated AF setting.

ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf194

INVICTUS randomized trial, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2209051

ACC/AHA valvular heart disease guideline, 2020 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000923
